newsitem.title: UK: Kissinger stars in television ad for The Economist.
newsitem.headline: Kissinger stars in television ad for The Economist.

text.p: Henry Kissinger, the former U.S. secretary of state, is starring in a television advertisement for The Economist magazine, his first such appearance in Britain.

In the ad a businessman settles into his seat in the first class section of an airplane and is just getting comfortable when he looks up to see that Kissinger is about to sit down next to him. The ad ends with the line, "Ready for a good chat?"
The ad is intended to convince business travelers of the need to be well-informed about world events, by reading The Economist.
The ad with Kissinger, who served as secretary of state under President Richard Nixon, began airing Monday on the News at Ten on Britain's ITV network.
It will run for 10 weeks on both the ITV and Channel 4, Britain's two terrestrial, commercial television networks.

Andrew McGregor, marketing director of The Economist, said David Abbott, chairman of Abbott Mead Vickers Plc, came up with the idea for the ad. Abbott Mead Vickers is parent of the Abbott Mead Vickers BBDO advertising agency.
The ad is aimed at The Economist's target audience of business people in senior management and above.
The Economist, which is 50 percent owned by Pearson Plc, uses posters as its primary advertising medium, but runs television ads every two to three years.
"We'd been working with Abbott Mead Vickers for about 11 years," McGregor said. "In January we said we were thinking about television for the autumn."

McGregor declined to detail the budget for the 10-week television campaign, but said The Economist is spending more than one million pounds ($1.6 million) on advertising this fall, including television, posters and press.
The Kissinger ad is being shown exclusively in Britain, which accounts for 106,000 subscribers out of the magazine's worldwide, weekly circulation of 600,000.

It is possible the ad could be shown in other countries some time in the future, but it will not be shown in the United States, despite that country being the magazine's single largest market, with 273,000 subscribers. McGregor said the ad cannot be shown in the United States because Kissinger has "some other prior agreement" there.
Despite the novelty of Kissinger's appearance in the ad, it does not mark his debut in a television commercial. McGregor said Kissinger previously did a U.S. television ad for the New York Times.
